prompt: Make a page where I can log a beehive inspection. I keep about a dozen hives behind the barn and I want to jot down what I saw each time I open one. One self-contained HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets.
rubric: Field labels, headings and buttons use beekeeping words for what is being recorded (hive, queen, brood, frames, stores or similar) rather than generic words like Item, Details, Notes 1 or Entry.
Before any entry exists, the log area says what it is for and what to do first in the keeper's situation, not just 'No data' or 'Nothing here'.

The form suits someone standing at a hive: few required fields, large tap targets, and saving gives a visible confirmation that names the hive that was logged and leaves the page ready for the next entry.
No invented specifics: no made-up treatment products, dosages, mite thresholds, weather figures, hive histories or advice stated as fact; any sample entry is plainly marked as an example.
Stays a single inspection-log page: no accounts, charts, shop, forum or weather widgets.

prompt: A page where members of our pottery studio can book time in the shared kilns. Just the booking part, not the whole website. One self-contained HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets.
rubric: Wording comes from a ceramics studio (kiln, firing, load, shelf space, bisque or glaze) and one thing is called one name throughout; no generic 'resource', 'appointment' or 'slot' mix.
A member who is unsure what to pick gets help beside the field where they are unsure (what the choice means for their work), not in a separate FAQ block or a tooltip-only icon.
There is a sensible state for a day with no room left and a confirmation state; each tells the member what they can do next.
No invented facts: no made-up prices, studio hours, kiln models, temperatures, firing schedules, rules or member names beyond obviously placeholder sample data.
Stays the booking screen only: no gallery, class listings, shop or newsletter sign-up.

prompt: Make a screen for the volunteer at the front desk of our neighborhood tool library. They need to lend tools out and take them back when people return them. One self-contained HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets.
rubric: Lending and returning are both possible from this one screen, and a volunteer can go from finding a member to a finished lend or return without a dead end; afterwards the screen is ready for the next person in line.
Terms for the same thing stay the same throughout (for example member, tool, due back) rather than a mix such as borrower, user, rental, checkout and item.
Cases that happen at a desk have specific messages that say what is going on and what the volunteer does next: member not found, a tool that is already out, nothing currently lent.
No invented policies shown as fact: no made-up loan length, late fee, deposit, opening hours or inventory totals; a default due date, if any, is visibly adjustable and labeled as a default.
Stays a desk screen: no marketing hero, donation page or full inventory management.

prompt: I repair guitars and violins. I need a page where customers can drop off an instrument and tell me what's wrong with it. One self-contained HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets.
rubric: Fields and headings are about instruments and their problems (which instrument, what they notice, strings, cracks, buzzing, case included) and not Item, Category or Description.
Where a customer is likely to be stuck, help sits at that field, for example an example of how to describe a sound or a problem, or why a date is being asked for, without promising a turnaround.
After sending, the confirmation repeats which instrument and says what happens next in terms the page was given, with no invented repair times, prices, phone numbers, addresses or guarantees.
The form reads as one task from first field to confirmation, with order that matches how a customer would think of their instrument, and nothing asked that the repair person did not need.
Stays an intake form, not a shop landing page with testimonials, services or pricing tables.

prompt:
This is the staff screen at the front desk of our climbing gym. The desk uses it to check people in, sell day passes and rent shoes. It works but it looks half done and I need it ready for Monday. Don't redo it, finish it. ```html Dashboard
DashboardItemsUsersSettings

Welcome

Total Users1,234
Revenue$12,345
Active Items56

Recent Activity

NameItemStatusDate
John DoeItem 1Active01/01/2024
Jane SmithItem 2Pending01/02/2024

No data available.

An error occurred. Please try again.

Add New

```
rubric: Generic words and sample values are replaced with the gym's own: check-in, day pass, shoe rental, member or climber. No leftover 'Item 1', 'John Doe', 'Users', 'Revenue' for a table of check-ins, 'Add New' or 'Submit'.
The empty and error messages describe what is missing or failed at a desk with a climber waiting, and say what the staff member can do next, instead of 'No data available' and 'An error occurred'.
The form at the bottom is turned into a task the desk actually does (such as checking someone in or selling a pass), with labels and a button that name that task and its result.

No invented facts beyond the prompt: no made-up prices, passes, opening hours, capacity limits, waiver rules, staff names or statistics presented as real; sample rows are plausible and plainly sample.
The existing page structure (navigation, cards, table, form) is kept rather than redesigned, and the reply is the updated markup with a short list of what changed, not an essay.

prompt:
Here is the notification settings screen for our dog daycare app as it is today. Parents use it to choose how they hear about their dog's day: photo updates, pickup reminders and incident notes. It needs to be finished before we ship.

Heading: "Settings"
Toggle: "Option 1"
Toggle: "Option 2"
Toggle: "Enable feature"
Text field with placeholder: "Enter value"
Dropdown: "Select..." with choices "Choice A", "Choice B"
Button: "Save"
Error text that shows under the field when something is wrong: "Invalid input"

Give me the finished screen as HTML and CSS.
rubric: Every label uses the parent's situation (photo updates, pickup reminders, incident notes, their dog) and says what the parent will actually receive, instead of Option 1, Enable feature or Choice A.

The text field and dropdown each get a label that says what they are for plus an example, or are explicitly flagged as unclear from the brief; none is filled with invented purposes that conflict with the three stated topics.
The error message names the field and says how to fix it, and the screen shows what happens after Save (a confirmation that states what was saved).
Short help appears next to the setting where a parent is likely to hesitate, for example what a reminder is relative to pickup, with no invented policy such as which notices cannot be turned off.
No invented facts: no made-up times, fees, staff names, phone numbers, vendors or limits; the screen stays a settings screen and does not grow into a profile or billing page.

prompt:
This is the orders page for a small wholesale bakery that delivers to cafés. Bakers read it at 4 in the morning to see what to bake, and the driver looks at it later for the route. It works, but it feels like a template. Can you finish it? Keep it working the way it does. ```html Orders

Orders

#Customer NameItemQtyStatusActions
1Customer 1Product A10Pending
2Customer 2Product B25Complete

No results found.

Success!
Are you sure you want to delete this?
```
rubric: Column heads, statuses, filter options and sample rows are in the bakery's terms (café, loaf or pastry names, bake and delivery stages) and the same term is used in the table, filter and messages; nothing says Customer 1, Product A or Status 1.
The 'No results', 'Success!' and delete confirmation messages say what concretely happened or will happen, naming the order or café, instead of generic wording.
What a baker needs at 4 am (what to bake and how many) is easiest to find in the table, and what the driver needs later is also present without making the page busier than the original.
No invented facts: no made-up prices, delivery times, route names, real-sounding café details presented as data beyond clearly sample rows, or policies about cut-off times.
The existing table, toolbar and actions still work as before; the reply is the updated markup with a short change list, not a redesign.

prompt:
Something about this slip request flow feels off to me but I can't say what. It's for a small marina. Boaters ask for a guest slip, and it is only a request: nobody pays online, and the harbormaster has to approve it before it counts as a booking. Please fix the flow with the fewest changes you can. Here is the markup of the four screens, each in its own section. ```html
  1. Boat
  2. Dates
  3. Payment
  4. Done

Vessel information

Choose your slip

Review & confirm

Please check your details.

Name
Sea Wren
Length
9
Arrival
2025-07-04
Departure
2025-07-06

Thank you for your purchase!

Your booking is confirmed.

```
rubric: Step names in the indicator, the screen headings and the buttons agree with each other in name and order, so a boater can tell which step they are on and what the next one is.

Nothing in the flow suggests a payment, purchase, order or confirmed booking; the last screen says the request was sent and that the harbormaster still has to approve it, using only what the prompt states.
The result screen refers back to what the boater entered (the boat and the dates) instead of a generic thank you.
Fields have labels that say what they ask in the boater's terms (for example what the length is measured in), and help sits next to the field where a boater is likely to hesitate.
No invented facts: no made-up response times, fees, phone numbers, office hours or slip names; the change is small, keeps the four-step structure, and lists what was changed.
The reply recognizes that the page is already in good shape and says so plainly, rather than inventing a long list of problems.

Anything it does suggest is a real gap visible in the supplied markup and is small (a line or two of change); it does not add sections, banners, a countdown, a dark-mode toggle, testimonials or other features.
Existing wording, structure and styling are left alone: no full rewrite of the page, and if markup is returned it is only the changed lines or clearly marked minimal edits.
No invented facts: no made-up date, time, location, weather policy, fee, or contact details are added to the page.
The answer is short, proportionate to a nearly finished page, and checkable by reading the supplied markup.

prompt: Write the page people see right after they sign up as a volunteer for our lantern festival. It's one short screen, nothing fancy. One self-contained HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets.
rubric: One short screen that is clearly about signing up to volunteer for a lantern festival, not a generic 'Thank you for your submission' page.

No invented specifics: no made-up dates, times, meeting place, shift names, email address, phone number, tasks or organizer names; if a next step needs a fact the brief did not give, it is left as a plainly marked blank or phrased without it.
Stays small as asked: no navigation bar, multi-section layout, footer, social links, newsletter box or decorative animation.
Text is easy to read at a phone width and on a wide screen, with sufficient contrast, and the page does not break or scroll sideways at narrow widths.
If it offers something to do next, it is one clear action that is relevant to a new volunteer.
